steps.name: Atom intake lint: split compound, abstract entities, detect paraphrases, cluster
steps.what_they_did: OntoChat's repository contains a CQ extraction prompt (in a function that is commented out at HEAD 737b7cc) telling the model to split compound questions and replace real-world entities by general concepts; its active analysis module offers LLM paraphrase detection followed by LLM topic clustering, or agglomerative clustering over sentence embeddings. The CQ generator shipped in the Bench4KE repository adds abstraction control, terminology consistency and de-duplication instructions and returns clustered, typed JSON.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: four lint passes at intake, each writing LintIssue records per atom: (1) compound - more than one requirement in an atom; propose a split, the human confirms, the original stays as parent; (2) vocabulary terms or named instances inside a term-free atom; (3) duplicate_of - paraphrase detection (embedding pre-filter plus one LLM confirmation per candidate pair) so one change can cover both atoms; (4) a topic cluster per atom, used to batch Propose and to group the workbench list. Input: AtomSet. Output: lint issues and cluster ids on the blackboard.

steps.name: One index record per term and three labelled retrieval sources, including the growing artefact
steps.what_they_did: External ontologies are indexed as one text chunk per class or property (file, kind, local name, IRI, label, comment cut at 200 characters). Per table, the top-3 chunks are retrieved from each of three FAISS indexes - the growing core ontology (re-indexed every iteration), the documentation, the external ontologies - with a query made of table, class, column and FK-target names (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings).
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: the vocabulary index holds one record per term (IRI, kind, label, definition, domain, range, vocabulary, source); embedding text is built from those fields; an exact IRI lookup backs the 'term exists' check. Retrieve returns three separately labelled lists per atom: (A) base-profile elements of the atom's target class plus accepted and pending changes (prevents duplicates across atoms); (B) the source excerpt around the atom's source reference; (C) vocabulary candidates. k per source is configurable (RIGOR uses 3).

steps.name: One requirement per call with a memoryless context; merging is engine work
steps.what_they_did: Memoryless CQbyCQ handles one competency question per call; the prompt slot for previously generated RDF is always empty and the story contains no other questions, which the authors say reduces the context considerably. How the per-question outputs are combined was not confirmed (the README mentions merging only for Ontogenia).
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: one Propose call per atom (or per small duplicate cluster) with only that atom, its source excerpt, the retrieved candidates and the base-profile slice of the target class. The accumulated change set is never pasted in as free text. Merging and conflict detection are deterministic (consolidate stage). Because the paper's expert sheets show duplicated classes in memoryless outputs, we pair this with retrieval over pending changes (G1-S02, list A).

steps.name: Fixed decomposition procedure: subject / predicate / object / value, then explain and rate confidence
steps.what_they_did: Ontogenia gives the model a nine-step metacognitive procedure: understand the question, identify the context, split it into subject, predicate, object and predicate nominative and map these to class, object property and datatype property, test subclass relations, add restrictions, add equivalence and disjointness, integrate, confirm and explain the reasoning, rate confidence and test on instances.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: the Propose system prompt carries a fixed numbered procedure: (1) restate the atom; (2) context = target class in the base profile; (3) split into subject / predicate / object / value type and map them to target_class, path, range class, range datatype; (4) decide reuse / refine / mint; (5) derive facets from the modality; (6) check against the base; (7) justify every facet and give a confidence. The decomposition is stored with the proposal so the reviewer sees how the atom was read.

steps.name: Answerability pre-check before proposing (already covered by the base)
steps.what_they_did: The Memoryless CQbyCQ prompt (inherited from the ESWC 2024 CQbyCQ prompt) tells the model to state, before writing OWL, whether the competency question is already answerable by the previous RDF and, if so, to return it unchanged; it adds that this is most likely (~90%) not the case. In the memoryless setting the previous-RDF slot is always empty.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: the first field the proposer fills is the atom's disposition (covered_by_base with references to the covering base elements, or needs_change); when covered, no change is emitted. Verify re-checks deterministically that each cited element exists in the base and that its facets satisfy the atom's modality, so a hallucinated 'already covered' fails. Our deviation: the prompt must not suggest a prior probability.

steps.name: Prompt anatomy with named sections, mandatory tasks, strict constraints and a common-mistakes footer; deterministic call settings
steps.what_they_did: RIGOR's generator prompt is a sequence of bracketed, named sections (direct mapping, schema, FK constraints, three retrieved contexts, correction instructions) ending in 9 numbered mandatory tasks and 7 strict constraints. Memoryless CQbyCQ ends with enumerated lists of typical mistakes per element type. GPT-4 was run with temperature and both penalties at zero so defined identifiers can be reused; OntoChat fixes temperature 0 and a seed.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: a prompt builder with fixed sections filled from typed inputs - [ATOM], [SOURCE EXCERPT], [BASE PROFILE SLICE], [PENDING CHANGES], [CANDIDATE TERMS], [CORRECTION INSTRUCTIONS], [MANDATORY TASKS], [STRICT CONSTRAINTS], [COMMON MISTAKES], [OUTPUT SCHEMA]; empty sections print 'None'. The mistakes list is a versioned file per change kind, extended from verifier failures and human rejections. Temperature 0, no frequency or presence penalty where exposed, fixed seed where supported. The rendered prompt and parameters are stored per call, so each section is inspectable on the workbench.

steps.name: Select reused terms from a closed candidate list, with an explicit way to abstain
steps.what_they_did: For dcat:theme the model must pick identifiers from an explicit list in the prompt and output only identifiers as a JSON array; the other property prompts fix their own output format. In the schema-miner repository's later QUDT grounding agent (follow-up work, not the ESWC 2025 paper) the model answers in a fixed JSON shape and is told to return 'cannot be grounded' when in doubt.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: the proposer may name a reused term only by choosing a candidate id from the list shown in the prompt (enum-constrained field in the output schema for path and range class); an IRI that is not in the list is rejected by Verify. An explicit abstain value with a reason per rejected candidate opens the mint path. Facet outputs have fixed types (integers, CURIEs, lists of concept IRIs).

steps.name: Reuse before mint, grounded only in retrieved evidence; a small pattern library
steps.what_they_did: RIGOR allows external alignments only when supported by retrieved external-ontology hints, and its judge asks that core concepts be reused, subclassed or aligned rather than duplicated. Ontogenia passes ontology design patterns to the model as named OWL snippets (JSON of name to pattern).
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: decision order enforced in the prompt and in Verify - reuse a base element, then reuse a retrieved vocabulary term, then refine or specialise, then mint - with a mandatory reason for every mint and the list of rejected candidates. A sub-property or sub-class link to an external term is accepted only if the target is among the retrieved candidates and exists in the index; we check this deterministically (in RIGOR's code the rule lives in the prompt and in a minor judge criterion only - our observation). A handful of named DCAT-AP extension patterns (add a property to an existing class; tighten cardinality; restrict a range to a controlled vocabulary; add a subclass with extra constraints) is offered as templates.

steps.name: Deterministic backbone first; the LLM only emits deltas; fall back to the backbone
steps.what_they_did: The direct mapping of each table is generated without an LLM and merged first, which guarantees schema coverage; the generator is told its role is semantic enrichment, not reconstruction; if no delta survives the retries, the deterministic mapping is kept and the run continues.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: the base DCAT-AP profile is loaded deterministically and is immutable. Model output is only ever a set of typed ProfileChange deltas. If an atom has no verified change after the repair rounds, the base stays untouched, the atom is marked unaddressed or pending review and queued for the human; the pipeline still compiles.

steps.name: A typed change record instead of model-written syntax; identifiers owned by the engine
steps.what_they_did: RIGOR has the model write Manchester syntax and reads it with a tolerant custom parser whose restriction rule accepts only 'some' and 'only'; other expressions fall through to a function that builds a named IRI. Memoryless CQbyCQ prescribes a 'Cl_' class prefix inside the prompt. Our observation in the released files: 62 distinct artefact IRIs such as #Genre_GenreId_exactly_1_xsd_integer in one stored RIGOR output, and the experts criticised the Cl_ prefix.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: the model fills the typed ProfileChange (JSON schema). LinkML, SHACL and DSV come only from the deterministic compiler. IRIs, prefixes and local names of minted terms are produced by the engine. No parser for model-written Turtle or SHACL exists, so no construct can be silently mis-read.

steps.name: Validate on a scratch copy (base + accepted + candidate) before committing; re-validate per unit and at the end
steps.what_they_did: An approved delta is parsed, added to a copy of the core ontology, and the copy is validated deterministically - restricted to the tables processed so far - before the delta is merged; the core is validated again after each table and once at the end, where an error aborts the run.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: Verify applies each proposed change to a scratch copy of (base plus included changes), runs the deterministic checks there and commits only on pass; checks are scoped to what has been processed (a change is not failed because other atoms are still open). The same checks run again after consolidation and once over the whole change set before compile; a final failure blocks release. Our deviation from RIGOR's order: deterministic checks run before any judge call, because they are cheap and objective.

steps.name: Coverage needs an executable witness
steps.what_they_did: A competency question counts as modelled if a SPARQL query extracting the answer can be written; the model returns Yes with the query, or No with a query for the partial answer; the ontology is read under a closed-world assumption.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: every coverage link (atom to change) gets a witness - a query over the compiled shapes graph (the property shape on the target class with the path and the facet values the atom requires) that must return a row. The witness is derived by rule from the typed change, not written by the model; a judge explanation may be attached. For partial coverage the link records what is missing. A coverage claim whose witness fails is downgraded to needs_review.

steps.name: Bounded repair loop with error-specific correction hints
steps.what_they_did: At most three generation attempts per table (MAX_JUDGE_RETRIES = 2). After a judge rejection the critical issues are fed back; after a deterministic validation failure up to 20 error messages are fed back; an empty response gets its own hint. The hint is a dedicated section of the next generation prompt.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: a repair call is the Propose prompt plus a [CORRECTION INSTRUCTIONS] section listing the failed check codes and messages (capped) and, if a judge rejected, its critical issues; unparsable output gets its own hint. Rounds are bounded by configuration (planned: 3); afterwards the change is set to needs_review and queued for the human; the repair round is recorded in the change's provenance.

steps.name: Judge contract: decision, severity-graded issues, corrected fragment; judge independent of the proposer
steps.what_they_did: RIGOR's judge returns one of three decisions (APPROVED, REJECTED, APPROVED_WITH_CORRECTIONS), issue lists in three severity tiers (critical, important, minor; 14 criteria) and a corrected fragment. Bench4KE's hit-rate evaluator raises an error when the declared tool model equals the evaluator model; RIGOR's evaluation judge is from another model family than the generators. Our observation: RIGOR's in-loop judge uses the same model client as the generator.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: a typed verdict - decision (approve, reject, approve_with_corrections), issues with severity, check id and message, optional corrected ProfileChange. Critical blocks and feeds Repair; important sets needs_review; minor is logged. A corrected change is a new proposal and must pass Verify. Configuration check: the judge model must differ from the proposer model; otherwise the workbench warns and the verdict is marked self-judged. Both model ids are stored with the verdict.

steps.name: Give the judge (and the reviewer) a verbalised slice of the profile
steps.what_they_did: A verbaliser lists classes with parents and comments, individuals, and relations with possible domains and ranges in plain text; each competency question is then tested with a Yes/No question, in one variant 'Yes/No, explanation', and the answer is parsed with a regular expression.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: the judge prompt is built from a deterministic verbalisation of the relevant slice only (for example: property P on class X, range R, at least 1, obligation mandatory, values from vocabulary V), not from raw SHACL. The same text is shown on the workbench, so judge and human read the identical statement. The answer starts with the label, then the explanation.

steps.name: Guardrails against over-trust in machine suggestions
steps.what_they_did: In the user study (19 participants, 20 tasks, half with an LLM suggestion) correct suggestions raised and incorrect suggestions lowered reviewer accuracy (+13% and -28% on the authors' slides) while overall performance did not change significantly. The authors name two mitigations: check the suggested SPARQL against the actual ontology before showing the label, and show calibrated confidence or provenance.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design for the workbench: (1) a machine verdict is shown as verified only when the deterministic checks and the coverage witness passed; otherwise it is labelled an unverified suggestion; (2) every card shows its evidence next to the label - witness, candidates considered, check results, votes agreeing of total; (3) the reviewer can answer 'cannot decide'; (4) decision, time and whether a suggestion was shown are logged, so over-trust can be measured later.

steps.name: Structured expert feedback (rubric and/or direct edit) re-injected into the next round; saved intermediates
steps.what_they_did: Three feedback methods - descriptive feedback under four headings (property merging, property grouping, missing properties, adequacy of descriptions), an expert-edited schema, or both - are passed as 'Domain Expert Feedback' into the refinement prompt; feedback is collected between batches of papers; the schema is saved after every iteration; the prompt demands a stable schema without overlapping additions.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: human decisions carry structured feedback codes besides free text - merge-with, retarget (class or path), missing requirement, wording - plus direct edit of the typed change. On re-run the feedback for the affected atoms is injected as a [HUMAN FEEDBACK] prompt section, together with a stability rule (accepted changes are not altered; no overlapping additions). Each stage run stores a snapshot of the change set on the append-only blackboard.

steps.name: Element-level provenance; a missing trace is a defect
steps.what_they_did: RIGOR attaches prov:wasDerivedFrom to every generated or modified class and property (pointing to the source table or column) and reports missing provenance as a validator warning. The ESWC 2025 ontology-generation study measured superfluous components - elements no requirement needs - at roughly 30% of generated classes and properties (slides).
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: every change lists the atoms it covers (atom id, reason, evidence quote) and every constraint carries its own justification; the compiler writes prov:wasDerivedFrom from each generated shape to the atom and emits the trace matrix. A change without a coverage link, or a facet without justification, fails Verify as an ERROR (RIGOR only warns). We report the superfluous-change rate - zero by construction in the full pipeline, measured in ablations.

steps.name: Preserved or strengthened: the delta may never remove or contradict the backbone; severity-graded rule catalogue
steps.what_they_did: Two critical judge criteria forbid removing or contradicting the deterministic mapping and require key, not-null and unique restrictions to be preserved or strengthened. The deterministic validator enforces coverage of the backbone, type consistency (no IRI both object and datatype property), exactly one domain and one range, XSD datatype ranges, and warns about missing label, comment or provenance.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: conformance compares every (target class, path) facet of the extension with the base and classifies it added / tightened / unchanged / loosened; 'loosened' or a missing base constraint is an error - our 'may tighten, never loosen'. Every rule has an id, a severity (error, warning, info) and a message; errors block, warnings go to review. Rules taken over: a path is not both object- and datatype-valued; datatype ranges are valid XSD; every element has label and definition.

steps.name: Score the verifier/judge as a classifier on a gold set with explicit negatives
steps.what_they_did: OntoChat tests its yes/no checker on 28 positive and 28 negative competency questions with a confusion matrix (our line count of the two files). OE-Assist uses 1,393 annotated question-ontology pairs (1,203 yes / 190 no in the CSV) and reports macro-F1 on the full, imbalanced set and accuracy on a balanced subset; the release holds three runs for two of its three models.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: a labelled set of (atom, change set) pairs with deliberate negatives - atoms the extension does not cover, wrong range or cardinality, changes that loosen the base (counterfactual atoms give paired negatives). Report macro-F1 on the full set, accuracy on a class-balanced subset and a confusion matrix for the Verify + judge stack; repeat LLM runs.

steps.name: Four-view quality evaluation including the superfluous-element rate
steps.what_they_did: Generated ontologies are evaluated in four views: pitfall scan with OOPS!, share of modelled competency questions (manual CQ verification by two ontology engineers), share of superfluous components (manual, two engineers), and expert evaluation by two experts with reported agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.61). The expert sheets record per question a status (ok/yes, maybe, no) and the element that addresses it.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: for every generated extension report (1) structural validity - SHACL-SHACL, profile lint, conformance report; (2) requirement coverage - share of atoms with a passing witness; (3) superfluous rate - share of added elements or facets no atom needs, judged by two annotators; (4) expert review with a fixed rubric (usability, completeness, accuracy; per atom yes / maybe / no plus the addressing element) and inter-annotator agreement.

steps.name: Threshold hit rate against a gold standard, facet-appropriate measures, no reliance on rubric scores alone
steps.what_they_did: Bench4KE's hit rate is the fraction of gold competency questions matched by at least one generated question with embedding cosine of at least 0.6, next to precision at the same threshold and lexical and semantic similarity metrics; an LLM judge rates items 1-5. The DCAT extraction study uses a different measure per value type (ROUGE and cosine for text, F1@k for keywords, fuzzy match for names, micro-F1 for controlled identifiers). Our reading of Bench4KE's stored result summaries: hit rate about 0.01 to 0.42 while the judge mean stays about 3.7 to 4.7.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: compare a generated profile delta with a gold delta by element-level hit rate - exact (target class, path) match for reused terms; for minted terms label + definition similarity above a calibrated threshold - plus precision at that threshold. Per facet: exact match for identifiers and counts, set-based micro-F1 for controlled vocabularies, text similarity only for definitions. Never use a 1-5 LLM rubric as the only quality signal, and never show gold items to a generator.

steps.name: Leakage controls: term masking and a protected benchmark
steps.what_they_did: mai2024adapt builds parallel datasets in which the lexical forms (and definitions) of WordNet concepts are replaced by gibberish and compares LLM performance on relation extraction and taxonomy discovery; per the abstract (via search, medium confidence) off-the-shelf models lean on lexical senses rather than reasoning over relations. lippolis2025ontology distributes its dataset in a password-protected archive to keep it out of training data.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: (1) a masked-term experiment condition - rebuild the vocabulary index with labels and IRI local names replaced by pseudo-words, definitions, domains and ranges unchanged; run the same atoms and compare reuse accuracy with the unmasked run; a large drop means the proposer relies on memorised DCAT knowledge instead of the retrieved definitions (finer-grained than hiding whole namespaces). (2) Publish gold atoms and gold extension in a protected archive. Design consequence: only retrieved candidates may be used (G1-S07).

steps.name: Ablations and baselines that keep the backbone constant
steps.what_they_did: RIGOR compares a direct mapping, a schema-only LLM baseline and a non-iterative RAG variant, and ablates each retrieval source in seven variants (no RAG; only or without schema/core context, external ontologies, documents) while always keeping the direct mapping. The Ontogenia script runs four trials (requirements only; plus patterns; plus procedure; all).
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: experiment conditions through pipeline switches with the base profile fixed: no retrieval; vocabulary only; base context only; no source excerpt; no judge; no repair; one call for all atoms versus one call per atom. Two baselines: base profile unchanged, and a single-prompt extension without verification. Score all conditions with G1-S20 to G1-S22.

steps.name: User-study protocols: counterbalanced assisted versus unassisted review, and blind side-by-side expert rating
steps.what_they_did: OE-Assist: each participant solves 20 verification tasks, half with an LLM suggestion, with a selectable order of the two conditions; answers Yes / No / I don't know plus a 1-5 difficulty rating; results analysed separately for correct and incorrect suggestions. RIGOR: experts see four anonymised ontology fragments per table (method names hidden), score each 0-5 on seven quality dimensions, rank them, and export the result as JSON.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: a workbench study with a fixed set of coverage decisions, half with and half without the machine suggestion, order counterbalanced; record accept / reject / cannot decide, difficulty and time; analyse accuracy separately for correct and incorrect suggestions. For output quality: anonymised extensions from different pipeline conditions rated side by side on fixed dimensions and ranked.

steps.name: Requirement atom register with LOT fields and a status lifecycle
steps.what_they_did: LOT ships spreadsheet templates for the requirement list with columns: Identifier (domain+id); Domain (domain template) or Sprint (use-case template); Competency Question / Natural language sentence (fact); Answer; Status (Proposed, Accepted, Rejected, Pending, Deprecated); Superseded by; Comments; Extracted from (provenance); Priority (High, Medium, Low). The CQ survey of 63 ontology engineers asked about benefits and difficulties and reports that guidance on CQs is limited (abstract level; the specific difficulties were not seen).
steps.how_we_reuse: RequirementAtom record = id, group, statement, subject, modality, optional example answer, status in {proposed, accepted, rejected, pending, deprecated}, superseded_by, comments, source reference (document, locator, quote), priority. Rules: only accepted atoms may be cited as coverage by a ProfileChange; splitting or rewriting an atom never edits it in place - the old atom is deprecated and points to its successor, so coverage links stay auditable. The workbench intake table is this register.

steps.name: Atom well-formedness gate from ISO 29148 individual characteristics and language criteria
steps.what_they_did: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 section 5.2.5 names nine characteristics of an individual requirement (necessary, appropriate, unambiguous, complete, singular, feasible, verifiable, correct, conforming) and has a section 5.2.7 on requirement language criteria. verify: the list of criteria (loopholes, ambiguous adverbs and adjectives, comparative and negative statements, vague pronouns, subjective language, and others) was confirmed only for the 2011 edition through a secondary paper. The SLR dataset records a study (Lubos et al. 2024) whose prompt classifies requirements against ISO 29148 quality characteristics with explanations and improvement suggestions.
steps.how_we_reuse: Two-layer intake gate. Deterministic checks: singular (one subject, one modality, no coordinated obligations), conforming (template fields present, modality from a controlled list), complete (subject, modality, object, source reference), term-free (no CURIEs or IRIs - our own atom rule), vague-term lexicon. LLM rubric: score 0-3 with a one-sentence rationale for necessary, unambiguous, verifiable, appropriate, shown beside the atom. Failing singular, unambiguous or verifiable blocks the atom from Propose until a human splits, rewrites or overrides with a reason. A suggested rewrite creates a new atom version, never a silent edit.

steps.name: Requirement-set checks before proposing
steps.what_they_did: 29148:2018 has a separate section (5.2.6) for characteristics of a set of requirements; verify: secondary sources list complete, consistent, feasible, comprehensible and able to be validated. The ORSD guidelines include Task 6, validating the set of requirements, which looks for conflicts, missing requirements and contradictions (who carries it out was not confirmed).
steps.how_we_reuse: One set-level report per atom set, computed before Propose: near-duplicates (see G2-S11); contradictions (same subject and aspect with incompatible modality or cardinality - deterministic over the typed atom fields, then an LLM pass for semantic conflicts); terminology consistency against the pre-glossary; a completeness question to the human with the base profile's classes as a checklist. Each conflict becomes a blocking review item because no ProfileChange can satisfy both atoms.

steps.name: Requirement-kind routing
steps.what_they_did: Glinz identifies definition, classification and representation problems with 'non-functional requirement' and proposes a concern-based taxonomy: functional requirements, performance requirements, specific quality requirements, constraints. He defines a non-functional requirement as an attribute of or a constraint on a system. verify: the claim that classification must not depend on representation.
steps.how_we_reuse: Add a kind field to atoms with a profile-specific mapping (our design, not Glinz's): content (what must be describable -> class or property changes), constraint (obligation, cardinality, range, value set -> constraint modifications), quality-of-profile (labels, IRIs, documentation -> profile-level checks, not term proposals), out-of-scope. The router sends only content and constraint atoms to Retrieve and Propose. Kind is assigned on the normalised intent, and the classifier's rationale is stored.

steps.name: Extension brief modelled on the ORSD
steps.what_they_did: The ORSD template as distributed by the LOT group has slots for purpose; scope; implementation language; intended end-users; intended uses; ontology requirements split into non-functional and functional; and a pre-glossary (terms from CQs with frequency, terms from answers with frequency, objects). The LOT version marks implementation language, end-users and pre-glossary as optional and allows requirements as CQs or sentences; verify whether the 2009 paper does. In LOT the ORSD is the output of requirements specification.
steps.how_we_reuse: ExtensionBrief record created before any LLM call: purpose; scope (base profile and version, classes in and out of scope); target languages (LinkML, SHACL, DSV); intended users and uses; non-functional requirements for the extension (namespace policy, naming conventions, reuse policy); grouped atoms; pre-glossary. It is the first workbench page, is prepended to every prompt as context, and is exported with the ProfileChangeSet as its human-readable specification.

steps.name: Pre-glossary terms with synonyms as retrieval queries
steps.what_they_did: The ORSD pre-glossary lists terms extracted from CQs and from answers with their frequencies. LOT's ontology-reuse activity extracts terms and their synonyms from the requirements or the data and uses them to search for existing ontologies that fit.
steps.how_we_reuse: Per atom, extract candidate terms (noun phrases -> concept candidates; verbal and prepositional phrases -> relation or attribute candidates), add synonyms, and use them as the top-k queries against the vocabulary index. Keep the term -> atom ids mapping and term frequency. A glossary panel on the workbench lets the human fix a term-to-concept binding once for all atoms that use the term.

steps.name: Reuse decision ladder derived from the NeOn scenarios
steps.what_they_did: NeOn frames ontology development as nine scenarios, including reusing ontological resources (whole ontologies, modules or statements), reusing with re-engineering, reusing with merging, reusing ontology design patterns, and restructuring ontological resources. verify: that restructuring covers modularising, pruning, extending and specialising, and that reuse guidance names search, assessment, comparison, selection and integration.
steps.how_we_reuse: Each ProfileChange carries reuse_path in {covered_by_base, specialise_base, reuse_external_term, reuse_extension_pattern, mint_new} plus a reuse_assessment list (candidate, source vocabulary, fit judgement, decision, reason). Verify rule: mint_new is illegal unless at least one retrieved candidate was assessed and rejected with a reason. This gives the planned 'reuse before mint with the reason stored' rule an explicit decision vocabulary.

steps.name: Extract the needed modelling primitives per atom before proposing
steps.what_they_did: To measure requirement complexity, an LLM extracts per competency question the minimal ontological primitives needed (concepts, properties, relationships, filters, cardinality hint, aggregation hint) plus reasoning into a typed pydantic schema; a flat-weighted count is the score. Stored notebook outputs show a weak negative correlation with the expert score, but the value differs between notebooks (overview.ipynb: -0.27, filters -0.29; cq_complexity.ipynb: -0.18, filters -0.20).
steps.how_we_reuse: A NeedAnalysis LLM call per atom before Retrieve: concepts, attributes, relations, value constraints, cardinality hint, rationale. Three uses: (1) retrieval queries; (2) a completeness checklist for Verify - each primitive must be accounted for by a ProfileChange element or by an existing base element; (3) an atomicity signal - an atom with a high primitive count is flagged as probably not atomic and offered for splitting.

steps.name: Modular, versioned prompt components with a stored generation configuration
steps.what_they_did: IDEA2 builds prompts from named components (role, definition, cross-domain examples, instruction, size limit, raw source) selectable at run time, requests schema-constrained JSON output, and stores each run's configuration (generation id, model, temperature, usage, role, prompt) in a separate table that every generated item links to.
steps.how_we_reuse: PromptSpec = ordered, content-hashed components (role, task definition, ProfileChange JSON schema, few-shot examples, instruction, extension brief, retrieved candidates, atom payload). GenerationConfig = provider, model, temperature, seed, component hashes. Every ProfileChange and every repair stores its generation_config_id. The workbench shows the exact prompt behind each decision; changing a component yields a new config id so runs stay comparable.

steps.name: More than one proposer; LLM drafts always go through refinement
steps.what_they_did: Five CQ sets produced from the same user story by different methods differ strongly in expert acceptance (repository notebook output: HA-1 90.9%, HA-2 98.1%, Pattern 50.0%, GPT-4.1 84.6%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 66.7%) and barely overlap semantically (bidirectional coverage between any two sets 0 to 15.3% at threshold 0.75). The abstract concludes that LLM output depends on the model and generally needs a refinement step. LLM runs used temperature 0 and seed 46.
steps.how_we_reuse: The Propose stage accepts several proposer configurations (different providers or models, optionally a rule-based proposer for routine cases). Proposals are unioned, deduplicated and labelled with their proposer. No proposal skips Verify and human review. Default temperature 0 and a fixed seed where the provider allows. The evaluation reports acceptance per proposer.

steps.name: Near-duplicate detection with two similarity bands
steps.what_they_did: IDEA2 embeds generated questions with all-mpnet-base-v2 and removes any whose cosine similarity to another exceeds 0.95 (optional, first iteration). AskCQ uses Sentence-BERT embeddings and a threshold of 0.75 to decide whether a question in one set is covered by another set, and reports novelty.
steps.how_we_reuse: One similarity service with three uses: atoms against atoms (intake duplicates); proposed terms against each other; a proposed new term's label and definition against the base profile and the vocabulary index, to catch a minted duplicate of an existing term. Two bands: >= 0.95 -> merge suggestion; 0.75 to 0.95 -> 'possibly covered', a reuse candidate the proposer must assess (G2-S07). Flag and keep the record; never delete silently. Both thresholds are starting values to calibrate on our data.

steps.name: Review ledger with votes, score, comments and priority per item
steps.what_they_did: IDEA2's dashboard holds one row per item with voters for and against, a computed score and vote count, a priority label, a comment thread, a link to the item it reformulates and a recap of the original item and its feedback. The score is a simple majority; score <= 0 means the item goes back for reformulation. Only the domain experts accept.
steps.how_we_reuse: ReviewLedger per ProfileChange: reviewer, decision (accept, reject, needs change), reason code, comment, priority, timestamp, version reviewed. Decision rule is configurable: single reviewer, or panel majority with a tie counting as not accepted. Any LLM judge verdict is stored as a separate advisory column and never counts as a vote, so the human keeps the final right. A recap card shows what a revised change replaces and the earlier comments and votes.

steps.name: Repair prompt driven by structured feedback, scoped to rejected items, one-for-one by id
steps.what_they_did: The reformulation prompt explains how items were evaluated (N experts, majority score), states that unlisted items were accepted and count as good examples, restricts the model to the rejected items, forbids new ones, and passes the rejected items as JSON with votes, score and comments (a default instruction is inserted when no comment exists). One mode requires each output to carry the original id; the standard mode pairs outputs with inputs by position.
steps.how_we_reuse: RepairRequest = list of {change id, version, failed checks (rule id, message), reviewer feedback (reason code, comment), atom payloads, allowed edits}. Prompt rules: fix only the listed changes; exactly one output per change id; echo the id; create nothing new; accepted changes are given as in-context exemplars. Post-validation rejects a response whose ids are missing, duplicated or new, which avoids positional pairing. At most three rounds, then the human review queue with the full history.

steps.name: Explicit, configurable stopping criteria for the review and repair loop
steps.what_they_did: The IDEA2 workflow figure names four stopping criteria for the iterative loop: a share of CQs accepted, a maximum number of iterations, a number of edits, and an expert time quota.
steps.how_we_reuse: LoopPolicy = max repair rounds (3), acceptance target, max edits per change, reviewer time budget. The engine records which criterion ended each loop. Unresolved items go to the human review queue marked 'unresolved after n rounds'; nothing is dropped.

steps.name: Version lineage and PROV-style export for every generated item
steps.what_they_did: Each reformulated item is linked to its original through a Reformulates relation; texts are identified by SHA-256 hash; the export is JSON-LD using OWLUnit CompetencyQuestion, PROV-O (wasGeneratedBy, wasAttributedTo a SoftwareAgent, generatedAtTime), schema.org and Croissant, with model, temperature and iteration per item.
steps.how_we_reuse: ProfileChange versions chain through a revises link, each with a content hash. The ProfileChangeSet exports with PROV-O: each added or modified element prov:wasDerivedFrom its atoms, prov:wasGeneratedBy a propose or repair activity carrying its generation configuration, prov:wasAttributedTo the LLM agent and the approving human; the 'why' text travels with the derivation. The workbench shows a lineage timeline per element.

steps.name: Four-level coverage rubric with a mandatory rationale on every atom-change link
steps.what_they_did: AskCQ has an LLM rate each question's relevance to the source user story on four levels with a rationale: 4 explicitly expressed; 3 inferable with common sense or domain knowledge; 2 not inferable but an enabler; 1 an extra, unnecessary requirement. Three prompt variants were tried on a subset. Stored outputs show the rating shifting with model and prompt. The CQ survey finds CQs are used mainly to define scope and evaluate the conceptualization (medium).
steps.how_we_reuse: Each covers link (ProfileChange -> atom) carries coverage_level and why: 4 = the atom explicitly demands this element; 3 = necessary to realise the atom though unstated; 2 = enabler only; 1 = not required. A change needs one link at level >= 3 to be eligible; level-2-only changes need human confirmation; level 1 is scope creep and is rejected. The proposer writes the rationale, an independent judge call re-rates, and disagreements go to the human. The atoms x changes matrix is the final traceability artefact; atoms without a level >= 3 link are reported as uncovered. Calibrate the rubric and keep human spot checks.

steps.name: One executable check per requirement, with paired acceptable and unacceptable data
steps.what_they_did: LOT includes an optional step that formalises functional requirements into a test suite. The AnIML ontology, whose requirements were elicited with IDEA2, ships one SPARQL query per validated question (102 files, each headed with its CQ number and text) and, for negative requirements, a SHACL shape with an acceptable and an unacceptable data file.
steps.how_we_reuse: Compile emits, per accepted ProfileChange, a SHACL shape fragment, a minimal conforming instance and a minimal violating instance, each annotated with atom ids. Checks: the shape accepts the first and rejects the second, and the conforming instance also validates against the base DCAT-AP shapes. That makes 'may tighten, never loosen' testable per change and makes each atom verifiable.

steps.name: Structured review checklist instead of a comment box alone
steps.what_they_did: A systematic review of empirical studies found that interviews, preferably structured, appear among the most effective elicitation techniques, that card sorting, ranking and thinking aloud tend to be less effective, and that analyst experience does not appear to be a relevant factor. The authors caution that the underlying studies were not replicated.
steps.how_we_reuse: By analogy (our design): the reviewer panel asks a fixed question set per ProfileChange - does it cover the cited atom; is the reused term semantically right; right class, domain and range; is the cardinality justified by the atom's modality; was a reuse alternative wrongly rejected. Answers are coded with an optional comment, and reject reasons come from a codebook. Coded answers feed the repair request (G2-S13) directly and make reviewers comparable (G2-S21).

steps.name: Assumptions queue and example instances to surface tacit knowledge
steps.what_they_did: Sutcliffe and Sawyer review elicitation through known knowns, known unknowns, unknown knowns and unknown unknowns (with Common Ground theory), find elicitation techniques relatively mature, and propose a research roadmap. Gervasi et al. review views of tacit knowledge across disciplines and propose a conceptual framework for RE that characterises its facets. verify: the role of scenarios and prototypes, and the working definition of tacit knowledge.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our design: (1) each ProfileChange lists assumptions - anything the LLM relied on that no atom states - and assumptions form their own review queue; (2) the workbench renders a small example record for each change so a domain reviewer reacts to something concrete; (3) open issues are typed as question for stakeholders, unconfirmed assumption, or out-of-scope discovery; (4) a list of base-profile areas no atom touches hints at what nobody asked about.

steps.name: Simulated stakeholder walk-throughs to find missing atoms
steps.what_they_did: Elicitron generates diverse simulated user agents (serially in one context or in parallel, with diversity sampling), has each simulate product use while logging Action, Observation and Challenge, interviews them, and has an LLM classify needs as latent using supplied criteria and chain-of-thought. It reports more latent needs than a human interview baseline.
steps.how_we_reuse: Optional gap probe, off by default. Generate a small diverse set of catalogue stakeholders (publisher, portal operator, data consumer, steward, domain specialist) in one serial call; each walks through tasks against the draft extension (describe, find, assess, access, cite) and logs challenges. Challenges become candidate atoms with origin 'synthetic' and no source reference; they cannot be cited as coverage until a human attaches a real source or accepts them explicitly.

steps.name: Agreement statistics when two or more reviewers judge the same items
steps.what_they_did: AskCQ computes Fleiss' kappa for three annotators from aggregated accept/reject scores (overall 0.354 in the stored notebook output, with 79% of items accepted). IDEA2's tool computes pairwise Cohen's kappa and Krippendorff's alpha on items rated by all raters. The IDEA2 workshop paper reportedly adds Gwet's AC1 and PABAK (search summary, medium).
steps.how_we_reuse: The evaluation module computes Cohen or Fleiss kappa and Krippendorff's alpha over review decisions, plus AC1 and PABAK because acceptance-heavy data depress kappa. Results are reported per run and per change type (add class, add property, modify constraint).

steps.name: Process metrics per review round
steps.what_they_did: IDEA2 offers per-iteration metrics: accepted total, share of items each annotator answered, number of comments, negative-score statistics. The workshop paper reportedly gives cumulative acceptance of 92.7% over 110 total validation tasks for the AnIML case, starting from 103 CQs with 95.1% first-iteration acceptance (search summary, medium).
steps.how_we_reuse: Log and report first-pass acceptance of ProfileChanges, acceptance after each repair round, review events per accepted change, comments per change, reviewer coverage, field-level human edits and time to decision. These are the process measures for the workbench study.

steps.name: Label each LLM call with the review's prompting-strategy categories, ablate, publish a replication package
steps.what_they_did: The review defines eight prompting-strategy categories; the replication workbook counts them over 74 studies (multi-label): zero-shot 28, few-shot 20, reasoning and task decomposition 16, context-rich 15, template-based 13, iterative 11, RAG-driven 4, interactive 3. 56 of 74 evaluations are laboratory experiments, 10 judgment studies, 5 field studies, 3 experimental simulations. The paper reportedly states 61% of studies share source code and prompts while shared datasets are scarce (search summary, medium); the share citing prompting guidelines was not confirmed.
steps.how_we_reuse: Tag every pipeline call with these categories: Retrieve = RAG-driven; Propose = template-based, context-rich, few-shot; Repair = iterative; workbench = interactive. Plan ablations that switch each off (no retrieval; free text instead of the typed record; no repair loop; no human feedback). Add a judgment study with two or three experts next to the quantitative comparison. Ship prompts, configurations and data as a replication package.

steps.name: Role-scoped pipeline rather than free agent conversation
steps.what_they_did: The review covers 50 primary studies on generative AI for RE, of which 24 describe an agent architecture (single agent or multiple role-based agents), maps them to the SWEBOK V4.0a requirements activities, and concludes that research on AI agents in RE is at an early stage.
steps.how_we_reuse: Architecture decision record: a fixed pipeline of narrow roles - retriever, proposer, deterministic verifier, repairer, optional judge - each mapped to one RE activity (analysis -> need analysis; specification -> ProfileChange; validation -> verify, judge, human review; tracing -> coverage links), with typed, stored messages between roles. Autonomy stays low: no role can accept its own output.

steps.name: LOT activity flow as workbench phases, with a verified-atoms gate and a maintenance loop
steps.what_they_did: In LOT, requirements move from proposed (early stage) to verified by domain experts and users before ORSD formalization; implementation proceeds in sprints over prioritised requirements (conceptualization, reuse, encoding, evaluation); maintenance feeds bugs and new requirements back into the proposal step.
steps.how_we_reuse: Workbench phases: Sources and scope -> Atoms proposed -> Atoms verified -> Brief -> Retrieve -> Propose -> Compile -> Conformance and tests -> Export. Propose consumes only verified atoms. Atoms are processed in priority-ordered batches so a reviewer never faces the whole set at once. A new atom or a reported defect opens a new ProfileChangeSet version; accepted elements are never mutated in place.

steps.name: Four-rung resolution ladder per requirement
steps.what_they_did: SEMIC resolves each use case by one of four standard situations, listed in this sequence: covered by DCAT-AP (reuse as-is); covered with adjustments (tighten only); covered by W3C DCAT, another vocabulary or another DCAT-AP profile (reuse that); not covered (new term in the profile's own namespace). Step 2 gives five worked examples whose field labels vary (Use case; Existing DCAT-AP solution, DCAT-AP solution or DCAT solution; Resolution or Approach). That older extensions follow the same sequence is our reading, not stated by them.
steps.how_we_reuse: Propose first emits resolution_case in {covered_as_is, tighten_base, reuse_other, mint}, then the facets. Mapping: covered_as_is -> AtomDisposition.covered_by_base; tighten_base -> refine_property; reuse_other -> reuse_property or reuse_class; mint -> mint_property or mint_class. The prompt presents the rungs as an ordered checklist and requires one sentence per skipped rung naming the candidate examined and why it fails. The six worked examples (CC BY 4.0) serve as few-shot exemplars in the same field layout. Verify rejects a later rung when an earlier rung had an undiscussed candidate (extends V4 to every rung).

steps.name: Tighten-only cardinality rule with upstream escalation
steps.what_they_did: Mandatory stays mandatory; a maximum of one stays one; stricter is allowed; a needed relaxation is raised as an issue on the base (GeoDCAT-AP did so for rights). mobilityDCAT-AP 3.0.0 notes one such case in its shapes header as to be reported to the DCAT-AP maintainers. HealthDCAT-AP states that mandatory properties retain their required status.
steps.how_we_reuse: V3 keeps the lattice test (new min >= base min, new max <= base max). A violation is not sent to Repair with the instruction to loosen. Repair may only drop the facet and inherit, move the need to another property, or mark the atom needs_review with outcome escalate_upstream and a drafted issue in the DCAT-AP template (submitter, product affected, problem or requirement, proposed solution).

steps.name: Range compatibility decision table (five cases)
steps.what_they_did: Five combinations of base range and required range with a verdict each: class to literal, not possible; literal to class, not possible; literal to literal, only a subtype; class to controlled vocabulary, fine; class to another class, only if semantically compatible, with double typing advised. Examples: contact point as text is impossible; release date restricted to xsd:date is fine, adding xsd:gDay is not.
steps.how_we_reuse: V2/V3 use a decision table keyed by (base kind, new kind). Needed data: an XSD derivation table plus the DCAT-AP union datatypes, and the subclass closure from the vocabulary index. The fifth case without subclass evidence yields status incomparable and goes to human review with the base class definition shown; on acceptance the engine adds a usage note recommending double typing.

steps.name: Controlled-vocabulary strength rules
steps.what_they_did: Four binding strengths. MUST: keep the vocabulary; other values need a separate property plus a mapping. At least one: keep one value from the original and add others. RECOMMENDED or MAY: another vocabulary may be used on the same property. First try to extend the vocabulary at its source. A different vocabulary goes on a different property (GeoDCAT-AP service category, HVD category, mobilityDCAT-AP mobilityTheme as subproperty of dcat:theme). DCAT-AP lists seven requirements for admissible vocabularies.
steps.how_we_reuse: Add cv_strength to the base element facets (filled from the DCAT-AP tables) and to Facets. Verify table: MUST plus a different list is an error with the repair hint to mint a subproperty of the base property, bind the new list there and add a mapping note. Admissibility of a proposed vocabulary (licence, maintainer, documentation, languages, URIs, persistence policy) is a warning checklist for the reviewer. Proposing missing values to the vocabulary owner is an escalation outcome.

steps.name: Semantic-fit test before reusing a base term
steps.what_they_did: Three outcomes when a term seems appropriate at first glance but its definition or usage note does not match the use: terminological difference only (relabel in the documentation); compatible but distinct (create a subclass or subproperty); significant difference (do not reuse, define new). The example is applicable legislation: legislation that mandates a dataset versus legislation that mentions it.
steps.how_we_reuse: A separate judge call per reuse or refine change. Input: the atom, the base label, definition and usage note verbatim, and the proposed usage. Output: same_meaning, narrower_compatible or different_meaning, with the base sentence that decides it. Effects: keep; convert to a mint with sub_property_of; convert to a mint without it. A split vote goes to the human queue. The quoted base definition is stored in the trace.

steps.name: Mint protocol: generic vocabulary term plus contextual profile usage
steps.what_they_did: A new property is defined once in a supporting vocabulary in a managed namespace, with open domain and range and a generic definition, and then used in the profile with class-specific notes and cardinality; vocabulary and profile are distinct specifications with their own lifecycle. mobilityDCAT-AP declares minted properties with rdfs:subPropertyOf, dcam:domainIncludes, dcam:rangeIncludes and a scope note. StatDCAT-AP logs each new property with range, cardinality and issue links.
steps.how_we_reuse: A mint change yields two outputs: a vocabulary entry (label, generic definition, sub_property_of or super_class when a nearest existing term exists, soft domain and range, rdfs:isDefinedBy) and the profile element with the facets. Lints: the definition must not name the target class; the IRI must be in the project namespace; label and definition are mandatory. Compile writes a separate vocabulary file next to the shapes.

steps.name: Derived reuse qualification A/E/P per element
steps.what_they_did: Property rows are tagged A, E or P in DCAT-AP 3 (relative to DCAT) and in the HVD annex, GeoDCAT-AP 3 and HealthDCAT-AP (relative to DCAT-AP). mobilityDCAT-AP 3.0.0 uses an extended scheme that also qualifies reuse from GeoDCAT-AP. The tag depends on the base version: DCAT-AP 3.0.1 changed one from extended to as-is after relaxing a cardinality.
steps.how_we_reuse: Compute it from the delta status, do not ask the LLM: unchanged -> A; tightened or added usage note -> E; not constrained by the base on that class -> P. Optionally record the origin of a P element (sibling profile, other vocabulary, minted). Show it as a column on the workbench and in generated documentation; recompute when the base profile version changes.

steps.name: Usage notes that state the change against the base and its reason
steps.what_they_did: mobilityDCAT-AP writes into the usage note of a changed element what changed relative to the named base version and why, marks additions with a plus sign, lists per class what is new, and gives an annex of all additions. The HVD annex names the legal article in the usage note of tightened properties.
steps.how_we_reuse: verbalise builds the note from FacetJustification: reason sentence, then the facet, the base value, the new value and the base id, then the atom ids. Documentation shows per class the blocks added by this extension and tightened, plus one annex table of all additions. The same sentence goes into sh:description of the property shape.

steps.name: Delta-only SHACL that imports the base shapes
steps.what_they_did: mobilityDCAT-AP shapes import the DCAT-AP shapes via owl:imports and contain only the deltas (inherit, do not re-encode). Files are split by kind of check; each property shape is a named resource with name, description, message and severity (Violation mandatory, Warning recommended and deprecated, Info optional). DCAT-AP publishes a variant with one IRI per constraint and a link to the specification anchor.
steps.how_we_reuse: Our compiler already writes deltas with prov:wasDerivedFrom to the atoms. Remaining: import the IRI of the base shape files, not the specification page (compile/shacl.py imports kb.base.info.homepage); optionally split into shapes, ranges, vocabularies and imports files with a versioned namespace each; give every constraint its own shape IRI from (class, path, facet); add sh:message and rdfs:seeAlso to the documentation anchor; decide on sh:Info for optional elements. Keep a self-contained file for validators that do not follow imports.

steps.name: Conformance by inheritance; the base wins and the case is escalated
steps.what_they_did: Conformance to the extension presupposes conformance to the base: DCAT 3 defines a profile that way, HVD and HealthDCAT-AP state it in their conformance sections, and with imported shapes it holds by construction. Where the base shapes are stricter than the extension intends, the stricter rule stays and is raised with the base maintainers.
steps.how_we_reuse: The Conformance stage reports three things: static (no facet loosened or in conflict), empirical (witness suites), and a list of escalations (atoms that cannot be met without loosening), each with the base constraint, the atom and a drafted upstream issue. The generated specification opens its conformance section with a sentence naming the base id and version. Checks C1 and C7 can cite these sources instead of calling the rule derived.

steps.name: Positive and negative witness suites, including base regression cases
steps.what_they_did: The mobilityDCAT-AP validation toolkit keeps test graphs per category, each split into positives and negatives with an id and the fault in the file name; a negative passes when the graph does not conform. The Data Cube development repository tests its integrity checks with a valid graph for the positive case and, for the negative case, either that graph plus a small delta graph or a separate failing graph named after the fault.
steps.how_we_reuse: C7 today generates one positive witness. Add for every included change one negative delta (the positive minus the newly required value, or with a value outside the range or list) that must fail under the extension, and a fixed set of base positives and negatives that must keep their verdict under base plus extension. Report per change: positive passes, negative fails, base verdicts unchanged. File names carry the change id.

steps.name: Requirement records with stable ids, tags and maintained back-links
steps.what_they_did: Use cases were written with a template (problem statement, stakeholders, suggested requirements; optional existing approaches, links, related cases), given stable ids and tags in four facets; requirements were derived from accepted use cases, deduplicated, given mnemonic ids, and linked in both directions to use cases and to a tracking issue; the document can be ordered requirements first.
steps.how_we_reuse: Atoms keep source_reference; intake adds optional use_case_id, stakeholders and tags from two facets (resource type for the class mapping; modelling aspect as retrieval hint and for clustering in Consolidate). Deduplication keeps the merged ids. The trace matrix is navigable both ways on the workbench (atom to changes to shapes, element to atoms) with two orderings.

steps.name: Requirement categories that route differently
steps.what_they_did: The requirements for the mobility profile were consolidated into forty requirements in four categories: General (8), Existing Vocabularies (5), Content (22), Implementation (5). Reported from search summaries; the texts were not opened.
steps.how_we_reuse: Intake classifies each atom. Content atoms go to Propose. Existing-vocabularies atoms configure Retrieve (preferred vocabularies and sibling profiles). General and Implementation atoms become run-level settings or get the disposition out_of_scope with the category as reason, so they stay visible. That only Content requirements describe information the metadata must carry is our reading.

steps.name: Information need first, mapping second, obligations side by side
steps.what_they_did: mobilityDCAT-AP first turned requirements into a technology-independent conceptual model, then checked each element against DCAT-AP, then against other vocabularies, changing usage notes and obligation levels where needed. GeoDCAT-AP prints the obligation of the source element and of the target property in the same table row. The Singapore Framework makes the domain model a mandatory component.
steps.how_we_reuse: Keep Propose in two passes. Pass 1 writes information_needed and a neutral description (entity, attribute, value kind, requested obligation) without IRIs. Pass 2 maps it to candidates and shows a two-column comparison requested versus base for obligation, cardinality and range. Pass 2 never receives pass-1 text that contains a term name.

steps.name: Issue-shaped proposals and a resolution log for human review
steps.what_they_did: SEMIC asks for one issue per use case with a problem statement and a proposed resolution or variants; the community agrees, disagrees or proposes an alternative, webinars with a vote are held when no consensus forms, and resolutions are recorded with the issues. The W3C group voted accept as-is, accept with changes or reject. StatDCAT-AP publishes a resolution log with issue, description, proposed resolution and final resolution. verify: SEMIC issue labels and the grouping of maintenance reports by change class.
steps.how_we_reuse: A review item shows the atom (problem statement), the proposed change (resolution), alternatives (variants) and failed checks. Reviewer actions: accept as-is, accept with changes, reject, defer, escalate upstream; each stores a reason. Export: a resolution-log annex in the StatDCAT-AP column layout and, for escalations, an issue text in the DCAT-AP template.

steps.name: Change impact classes and version bump
steps.what_they_did: DCAT-AP maintenance classifies each issue as bug fix, minor semantic or major semantic. The mobilityDCAT-AP governance chapter defines them: minor changes affect interoperability non-disruptively (for example optional additions); major changes include adding mandatory properties or a mandatory vocabulary; versions follow X.Y.Z. The mobilityDCAT-AP 3.0.0 migration guide sorts changes by what a provider must do.
steps.how_we_reuse: Classify each included change by rule: editorial -> patch; new optional or recommended element -> minor; new mandatory element, raised minimum, narrowed range or closed value list -> major. The change set gets the highest class and a suggested version. Compile emits a provider checklist with the categories MUST add, MUST restrict, MAY add.

steps.name: Change table and change-log sentences generated from typed records
steps.what_they_did: DCAT-AP 2.0.1 Annex II is a change table with URI, type, action, description, issue and release. StatDCAT-AP Annex II is a log of new properties with type, range, cardinality and issue links. mobilityDCAT-AP writes change-log sentences in a fixed form with the reason and the issue number.
steps.how_we_reuse: compile/docs.py renders two artefacts from the ProfileChange list with atoms in place of issues: a table (URI, type with obligation and owner class, action, description with range and cardinality, atoms, version) and sentences stating element, class, facet, old value, new value, reason and atom ids. No free text is written by the LLM at this point.

steps.name: Documentary completeness check of the compiled package
steps.what_they_did: The Singapore Framework defines an application profile as a documentation package: functional requirements, domain model and Description Set Profile are mandatory, usage and syntax guidelines optional, and the functional requirements are the basis for evaluating internal consistency. SEMIC's publication step lists the HTML specification (context, difference from DCAT-AP, contact), SHACL shapes and, for new terms, a vocabulary document and an RDF file.
steps.how_we_reuse: A final checklist in Compile, shown on the workbench: requirements (atom set with scope and out-of-scope atoms), domain model (class diagram of the extension against the base), constraints (SHACL, LinkML, DSV), usage notes for every added or tightened element, syntax (JSON-LD context), vocabulary file when anything was minted, statement of how the profile differs from the base. Missing mandatory parts block export. Every element must trace to an atom and every in-scope atom must have a coverage state.

steps.name: Coverage status per mapping and a core/extended split
steps.what_they_did: GeoDCAT-AP 1.0 classifies mappings as complete, partial (only mandatory components representable) or provisional (unstable, to be replaced when a standard term exists), and publishes two profiles: Core, consumable by plain DCAT-AP applications, and Extended.
steps.how_we_reuse: CoverageLink.coverage gains the value provisional (a term chosen for want of a better one, flagged for revisit and shown as unstable in the documentation). Compile can emit two views: core (reuse and tightening of base elements only) and full (with additions), so a reader sees what a plain DCAT-AP consumer will understand.

steps.name: Several usage contexts: subclass or sub-profile instead of conditional notes
steps.what_they_did: SEMIC: when one class is used in several contexts with different obligations, create a subclass per context; when a context spans several classes, make a separate sub-profile. HealthDCAT-AP publishes three obligation variants by access level with separate SHACL files; HVD is an annex because its context spans datasets, services and distributions. Both state that their shapes assume every resource is in scope.
steps.how_we_reuse: Intake extracts a condition from atoms. Consolidate groups atoms by condition. One conditioned class leads to a proposed mint_class as subclass with its own shape; a condition touching two or more classes leads to a named variant (separate shape file with its own target). Conditions are never encoded only in usage notes.

steps.name: Strong-recommendation pattern and the machine-verifiability rule
steps.what_they_did: For a requirement that is strongly recommended but not obligatory, the HVD annex kept the formal minimum relaxed, set the usage qualification to recommended, explained it in the usage note and added a SHACL check. DCAT-AP 3.0.1 says the two MUST levels for controlled vocabularies should be used only for requirements a machine can verify.
steps.how_we_reuse: The mapping from modality to constraint gets a middle path. should -> obligation recommended, no minimum, a Warning-severity shape and a usage note quoting the atom. A must atom whose condition no shape can test is downgraded to recommended plus usage note, with a trace note saying why, instead of becoming an unverifiable mandatory constraint. The default severity Warning is our choice; HVD uses Violation.

steps.name: Numbered integrity constraints as ASK queries with one failing fixture each
steps.what_they_did: The Data Cube development repository defines well-formedness as numbered integrity checks, each with a one-line statement and a SPARQL ASK query that is true on violation, and tests them with a valid graph and, for the failing case, either that graph plus a small delta or a separate failing graph. The Recommendation text itself was not read.
steps.how_we_reuse: Express the profile-level invariants of the change set (V5, C2 to C5) over an RDF rendering of the ProfileChangeSet as numbered queries with a statement each, for example every minted property has a label, a definition and a range, or no two included changes set different maxima on the same class and path. Each query ships with one failing fixture. The checks become inspectable on the workbench and citable by number.

steps.name: Base-level guards: inverse pairs, unlisted DCAT properties, no removal
steps.what_they_did: DCAT 3 allows the eleven listed inverse properties only in addition to the canonical ones. DCAT-AP treats DCAT properties it does not list as optional without conformance expectation. mobilityDCAT-AP 3.0.0 lists elements 'not used from DCAT-AP' where version 1.1.0 spoke of removed properties. verify: whether a reason is documented for each unused element.
steps.how_we_reuse: Three rules. (a) A table of the inverse pairs; a change that uses the inverse where the canonical property exists is rewritten or rejected. (b) Retrieve labels a DCAT property the base profile does not list as in DCAT, not constrained by the base, so it lands on rung three of the ladder. (c) No change kind removes a base element; an atom asking for it yields a usage_note change not used, with a warning that DCAT-AP receivers must still process it.

steps.name: Retrieval tiers and admissibility criteria for vocabularies
steps.what_they_did: The sources agree in outline on an order of preference: DCAT-AP itself first; related extensions and the vocabularies DCAT-AP already uses next; other well-maintained vocabularies after that; own terms last. Named admissibility criteria: persistence and versioning policy, cross-domain use, maintenance. No single source ranks sibling extensions against other vocabularies.
steps.how_we_reuse: The vocabulary index stores a tier per term: T0 base profile on the same class; T1 base profile on another class; T2 DCAT 3 outside the base; T3 sibling DCAT-AP profiles; T4 vocabularies the base already uses; T5 other admitted vocabularies. Retrieval boosts by tier and writes the tier into Candidate.why. A vocabulary enters the index with its admissibility fields (maintainer, licence, versioning policy); missing fields produce a warning on any change that uses it. The tiering is ours.

steps.name: Profile-level reuse metrics with reference values from published extensions
steps.what_they_did: Published extensions state or let one count how much was added and how much was newly defined: GeoDCAT-AP 1.0 defined no new terms; DCAT-AP-JRC 1.0 defines no own classes or properties; StatDCAT-AP 1.0.0 logs six new properties, four in its own namespace; mobilityDCAT-AP 1.1.0 states 2 additional classes and 48 additional properties, and its vocabulary file declares 2 classes and 12 properties in its own namespace (my count).
steps.how_we_reuse: Three run-level measures on every change set: mint rate (minted terms over added elements), tier distribution of reused terms, and the A/E/P distribution. The published profiles give orientation values, not targets. A mint rate far above them is a review signal shown on the workbench.
