steps.name: Blackboard triad: levelled record, independent knowledge sources, separate control
steps.what_they_did: Hearsay-II (per abstract-level and secondary sources): independent knowledge sources cooperate only through a global blackboard holding hypotheses at several levels; knowledge sources are invoked in response to blackboard changes; a scheduler / focus-of-control mechanism selects the next action. Nii 1986 describes the blackboard model and the more detailed blackboard framework. verify: the terms 'blackboard monitor' and 'condition-action', the 'most promising action first under limited resources' rule and Nii's three-component wording were not confirmed from the papers.
steps.how_we_reuse: BlackboardEntry stays the only channel between stages. Declare per stage the entry kinds that trigger it and the kinds it writes. Add a small scheduler that marks downstream entries stale when an input changes and orders the agenda (deterministic checks before model calls, then by uncertainty). Levels: atom, assessment, candidates, change, element, artefact, conformance. Human decisions are entries of the same kind.

steps.name: Decision matrix: a row per candidate, a column per knowledge source, each cell a vote with a reason
steps.what_they_did: SAST-Blackboard gives every candidate mapping a matrix row; the validator and four signal agents each write {accepted, reason} into it; the selection agent must read the matrix and accept exactly one candidate with a reason per candidate.
steps.how_we_reuse: Derive a matrix per atom from ProfileChange.verification, alternatives and the retrieved Candidate list: rows are candidate terms or alternative changes, columns are V1..V6, T1, the attribution judge and the reuse check; each cell stores passed, reason, author. The proposer's choice cites cells; the workbench shows the matrix as the main inspection view. Key cells by candidate id, not by position (their code aligns votes by array position).

steps.name: One self-contained, replayable decision record per run
steps.what_they_did: SAST-Blackboard writes one JSON per sample with the complete state and logs per attribute (including raw model answers), all discussions turn by turn, the list of changes caused by discussion and the evaluation before and after. FastChat stores for every judgement the full prompt, the full answer, judge model and prompt name, and a timestamp.
steps.how_we_reuse: One export bundle per project: atoms, assessments, matrix, changes with trace, every LLMCallRecord, every blackboard entry, human decisions kept apart from machine output, and the bundle hash in SignOff. It lets a reviewer re-check any decision without rerunning the model.

steps.name: Typed candidate, assembly by code, deterministic gate before any model judgement
steps.what_they_did: The model returns {object, relation, reason}; the prompt forbids writing the triple and code assembles it. A deterministic validator checks triple syntax, existence of class and property, property type and whether the sample's values fit the property's range; only validated candidates reach the signal agents and the selection.
steps.how_we_reuse: Confirms 'typed ProfileChange, never free SHACL' and 'verify before judge'. Additions: keep the per-check booleans with each candidate (their validator_meta) so the matrix shows why a candidate was dropped, and add a value-plausibility check where sample metadata records exist.

steps.name: Controls for non-determinism at call time
steps.what_they_did: Atil et al. (v2) showed that temperature 0, top-p 1 and a fixed seed do not give identical outputs on hosted models, that raw strings vary far more than parsed answers and that longer outputs are less stable. Ouyang et al. studied repeated requests at temperature 0, 0.5 and 1 (no seed setting seen). Authors' follow-up notebooks (not in the paper): a schema raises raw agreement but tends to reduce accuracy; strict structured output still varies in content; one local single-job model was deterministic in a single small experiment (1 task, 1 model, 10 runs of 100 questions).
steps.how_we_reuse: Keep the replay cache and treat the stored answer as the decision. Put every setting that changes the answer into request_hash and LLMCallRecord (at the snapshot read, temperature and the output limit are not in the hash). Store the model id returned by the provider. Compare decisions by signature, not text. Cap free-text field length. Offer a local single-job model as the reproducible configuration.

steps.name: Independent proposals with a majority vote as the default; no free debate
steps.what_they_did: Choi et al. score the majority vote over independent answers and after each debate round and conclude that voting explains most of the gain and debate alone does not raise expected correctness. Smit et al. find that debate does not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling and is more sensitive to hyperparameters, but also that tuned debate (for example by modulating agent agreement) can outperform the non-debate protocols they tested. Du et al., who report gains from debate, take the most frequent final answer in the GSM, MMLU and arithmetic scripts.
steps.how_we_reuse: PipelineConfig.votes with an odd N; majority over the normalised decision signature and 'no strict majority means needs_review' (both already implemented); never a random tie-break; keep all N answers so agreement metrics come for free; state in the paper that debate was deliberately not the default and why.

steps.name: If agents interact: selective, bounded, with a closed command set
steps.what_they_did: SAST-Blackboard lets a reasoning agent declare discussions only where needed, assigns weak and strong roles, and asks for a maximum of 3 turns by default (the value is passed through the model-written discussion record; the engine's own fallback is 4); turn 1 forbids commands and afterwards only Change:Candidate (index among the top-3 validated candidates) or DiscussionState:End are executed; outcome labelled Correction, Acceptance or No agreement. Choi et al. state at abstract level that interventions biasing belief updates toward correction make debate more effective.
steps.how_we_reuse: A council only for changes with split votes, an inconsistent judge or an open Conflict. Allowed actions: choose another already verified alternative, withdraw, end; no new terms or facets inside the council. Verifier results are shown as fixed facts. Max 3 turns, each turn a blackboard entry, outcome label stored, 'no agreement' goes to the human queue.

steps.name: Account for what interaction changed: corrected, harmed, unchanged
steps.what_they_did: SAST-Blackboard snapshots the selection before discussion, evaluates before and after, lists every change and counts per role whether a change was better, worse or the same. DebateLLM records per agent whether it changed its answer, was helped by others (relied_on_other) or was talked out of a correct answer (bullied_by_other), plus cost, time and tokens.
steps.how_we_reuse: For every repair round and council store the change hash before and after. With a gold delta report corrected (wrong to right), harmed (right to wrong), unchanged, and calls and tokens per corrected change. Use the counts to set repair_rounds and to decide whether a council exists at all.

steps.name: One explicit deference setting in interaction prompts, tuned on a development split
steps.what_they_did: Added a sentence that fixes how much an agent should adopt the other agents' opinions, in eleven levels, and treated the level as a hyperparameter; the README reports about 15% (Multi-Persona) and about 5% (Society of Minds) improvement on USMLE when it is tuned.
steps.how_we_reuse: Where a repair or council prompt shows another agent's or the judge's opinion, state how much weight it has with a small fixed set of wordings (verifier facts are binding; judge remarks are advice). Record the level in prompt_version. Tune only on a development split.

steps.name: Judge contract: evidence first, strict verdict, abstain and error as explicit values
steps.what_they_did: FastChat asks for a short explanation first and the verdict last in a fixed pattern, calls the judge at temperature 0 and records -1 or 'error' when the pattern is missing. FairEval's output template starts with 'Evaluation evidence:'. Du et al.'s fact check allows the answer 'uncertain' and excludes those answers.
steps.how_we_reuse: Order the fields of AttributionOut as explanation (starting with the atom's decisive words), unsupported_facets, verdict (the snapshot has verdict first). Add a verdict value cannot_judge that routes to review. Record an invalid judge answer as a failed call, never as unsupported. Compare evidence-first against verdict-only on the judge validation set, because Stureborg et al. found non-CoT prompting better for numeric scores.

steps.name: Order-swap consistency check
steps.what_they_did: FastChat judges each pair in both presentation orders and counts a win only when both runs agree; otherwise the result is a tie and the loader names the case 'inconsistent'. FairEval asks again with the two answers swapped and pools the scores.
steps.how_we_reuse: For every model decision over an ordered list (candidate terms, alternative changes, several atoms) run a second call with the order reversed or shuffled by a seeded permutation. Same decision: record order_consistent = true. Different decision: needs_review with both answers shown. Report the consistency rate per model as a quality figure of the judge.

steps.name: Several sampled judgements instead of one
steps.what_they_did: FairEval samples k judgements per order (default 3, temperature 1) and averages the scores. The released G-Eval GPT-4 script samples 20 short answers (temperature 2, max_tokens 5) and the meta-evaluation averages the parsed scores. verify: that this sampling is meant to approximate the paper's probability-weighted score.
steps.how_we_reuse: Judge each change k = 3 times through the client's variant mechanism; verdict by majority; store agreeing and total votes on the T2 check result. For graded criteria use the mean of the samples.

steps.name: Send the most disputed items to the human first
steps.what_they_did: Introduced a 'balanced position diversity entropy' to measure the difficulty of each example and sought human assistance for the difficult ones (human-in-the-loop calibration). verify: the exact definition of the entropy (over which judgements it is computed).
steps.how_we_reuse: Per change compute the entropy of the verdict distribution over k samples times 2 orders, combined with the vote split of the proposals; sort the review queue by it; allow auto_accept only at entropy 0 with all checks passed; show the split to the reviewer.

steps.name: One criterion per judge call, coarse scale
steps.what_they_did: G-Eval uses one prompt per criterion with the criterion's definition, numbered evaluation steps and a form to fill. Stureborg et al. (short version read) found that scores for earlier criteria bias later ones in the same generation, that a 1-100 scale collapses to a few round numbers, and that deterministic non-CoT prompting with a 1-10 scale worked best.
steps.how_we_reuse: Separate calls for separate questions (attribution of facets; adequacy of the no-reuse justification; quality of label and definition). Categorical verdicts or 1-10, never 1-100. Each judge prompt carries the criterion definition and the steps to follow.

steps.name: Batch-wise comparative pass for consistency across changes
steps.what_they_did: Judged 10 samples per prompt with the instruction to compare them, analysis of all samples before any score, decimal scores, 5 rounds with re-batching so each batch mixes quality levels, mean over rounds.
steps.how_we_reuse: A consistency knowledge source in the consolidate stage: batches of (atom, change) pairs that share a facet type are shown side by side; the model analyses all first, then flags unequal treatment (same modality but different obligation; same information need but different term). Re-batch once by the first verdict. Output is a list of Conflict candidates for review, not an accept/reject decision.

steps.name: Guard against a judge that favours its own kind of text
steps.what_they_did: G-Eval flags a potential bias of LLM evaluators toward LLM-generated text (abstract). Stureborg et al. (short version) measured a GPT-4 preference for low-perplexity summaries and note as an implication that evaluators may prefer self-generated text. The MT-Bench pairwise prompt forbids position, length and name bias. verify: that the MT-Bench paper reports a self-enhancement bias (abstract not re-checked).
steps.how_we_reuse: Configure the judge model separately from the proposer (step_models), prefer another model family, and record a check when they are equal. The judge sees the verbalised change and the atoms, not the proposer's rationale, so length and style cannot sway it. Add a term-masked condition in experiments to see whether familiar vocabulary names drive the verdict.

steps.name: The attribution test in two questions
steps.what_they_did: Defined attribution through an 'according to' test applied to a standalone proposition derived from the sentence in context (abstract-level and secondary sources), and annotated in two stages (primary data): first whether the output is interpretable, then, only if so, whether it is fully attributable to the source; five annotators, majority label, agreement count stored, a flag for malformed items that cannot be judged. verify: the term 'explicature'.
steps.how_we_reuse: The verbaliser produces a standalone sentence per facet ('According to atom A-12, datasets must state ...'). Check T2 asks Q1 (understandable?) then Q2 (fully attributable to the cited atoms alone?) with two-valued answers; Q1 failures go back to the verbaliser or mark the change unclear. The human review form uses the same two questions and stores how many reviewers agreed.

steps.name: Trace recall and trace precision with a leave-one-out test
steps.what_they_did: Recall is 1 for a statement iff it has a citation and all its citations together entail it; a citation is irrelevant iff it alone does not entail the statement and the remaining ones still do; precision counts the non-irrelevant citations of fully supported statements; missing or unknown citations give recall 0 without a model call; redundant supporting citations are not punished; partial support is a stated blind spot.
steps.how_we_reuse: Statement = one facet justification, citations = its atom_ids. T1 (atom exists, verbatim quote) gates T2. T2 per facet: joint support by the cited atoms gives recall; for facets with more than one atom and recall 1, one extra call per atom gives precision. Report trace recall, trace precision, share of multi-atom facets and of superfluous links. Recall failure is an error, a precision failure a warning. Allow humans a third label 'partially supports' in the validation study.

steps.name: Break ties among sampled proposals by support, not by self-confidence
steps.what_they_did: RERANK: sampled four answers per question and kept the one with the best automatic citation recall, at n times the compute; the paper reports that reranking boosts citation quality as measured by human evaluation, and notes that human and automatic scores diverge for RERANK, which uses the automatic recall for selection. verify: that correctness was unchanged.
steps.how_we_reuse: Optional policy when the votes show no majority: prefer the proposal with the highest trace recall, mark it 'selected by support' and still queue it for review. Never report trace recall as an independent result for runs that used it for selection.

steps.name: Validate the judge against humans before trusting it
steps.what_they_did: MT-Bench compares judge-human with human-human agreement, with and without ties (README: over 80%). ALCE reports Cohen's kappa (0.698 recall, 0.525 precision) and accuracy (85.1%, 77.6%) of the automatic metric against human labels, plus precision and recall for detecting the bad cases. AIS stores per item how many of five annotators agreed.
steps.how_we_reuse: A study of about 100 (facet, atom) links sampled across verdicts; two reviewers label them with the two attribution questions. Report human-human agreement, judge-human agreement, Cohen's kappa, and the judge's precision and recall for 'unsupported'. Repeat when the judge model or JUDGE_VERSION changes. This table is what licenses automatic acceptance.

steps.name: Stability report: TARr, TARa, min/median/max, best-possible and worst-possible
steps.what_they_did: Defined total agreement over N runs on raw output (TARr@N) and on parsed answers (TARa@N); reported min, median, max and spread instead of mean and deviation because the variation is not normal; added best-possible and worst-possible accuracy. Ouyang et al. measured agreement of behaviour (same test outputs), of text and of structure over five requests under three temperatures and two request ways.
steps.how_we_reuse: A command that reruns a project N times without the cache and reports per atom and overall: TARr (identical raw answer), TARa (identical decision signature), element-level F1 as min/median/max, and F1 when an element counts if produced in any run or only if produced in all runs. Publish N, the model id and settings with every result table. Behavioural analogue: do the compiled shapes of two runs accept and reject the same test records.

steps.name: Contamination probe and registry entry per model and gold profile
steps.what_they_did: Asked the model to regenerate a benchmark split, labelled the outcome contaminated, suspicious or clean per split, required the number of attempts and evidence, and collected the results in a public registry; the paper argues that conclusions from contaminated settings should be flagged.
steps.how_we_reuse: A pre-run step asks the configured model, without atoms, what a named gold profile adds to or tightens on its base; overlap with the gold delta decides the label; prompt, attempts, answer and label become a project-level blackboard entry and a row in the paper's contamination table. Report results per label. Counterfactual atoms (Atom.counterfactual_of) test whether output follows the requirement where it contradicts the remembered profile.

steps.name: Score on judged items, report the unjudged share, pool outputs for adjudication
steps.what_they_did: Buckley and Voorhees introduced bpref, which uses only judged documents and makes no assumption about unjudged ones; trec_eval also reports the unjudged share as a red-flag measure. Zobel (abstract level) showed that pooled judgments compare systems fairly while absolute recall is overestimated because relevant items outside the pool exist.
steps.how_we_reuse: Treat the gold profile as an incomplete judgment set: a generated element absent from it is unjudged, not wrong. Per condition report strict precision, judged-only precision after expert adjudication, and the unjudged share. Adjudication pool = union of generated elements of all conditions, de-duplicated and blinded. Label recall against the gold delta as an upper estimate. Flag, do not rank, a condition with a high unjudged share.

steps.name: Show that conclusions survive a change of judge
steps.what_they_did: Built alternative relevance judgment sets from different assessors, including union and intersection, and showed with Kendall's tau that system rankings stay highly correlated although the judgments themselves differ substantially.
steps.how_we_reuse: With two reviewers, score all pipeline conditions under reviewer A, reviewer B, their union (lenient) and intersection (strict); report the four rankings and Kendall's tau between them plus plain inter-reviewer agreement. State that the claims are comparative and name the comparisons that hold under all four sets.

The link between the paper and github.com/U0iS112/654321 rests on that repository's own README ('SimpleLLM & SAST Blackboard') and on the blackboard-workbench README; the paper text was not seen by me either. My search confirms title, the SDS 2026 workshop and the general idea (signal agents, shared blackboard, selection and discussion) from announcements only.

smit2024mad: the summary gives only half of the abstract. Per my search the abstract also says that with hyperparameter tuning, in particular modulating agent agreement, some debate set-ups (Multi-Persona) can outperform the non-debate protocols tested. The repository's BibTeX lists Smit, Duckworth, Grinsztajn, Barrett, Pretorius (confirmed in README l.141); the bib entry uses the PMLR order.

atil2025nondeterminism: the 'single-job local model was deterministic' notebook is one task and one model (10 runs of 100 college math questions, 'deterministic so far'). A third-party summary of the paper mentions five reruns while the v5 abstract says 10 runs; check the methods section before citing the run count. The 'token probabilities did not predict instability' claim was not re-verified (only the notebook's question and set-up text were read).

rashkin2023ais: 'explicature' is not confirmed by any source I saw; search results speak of a 'standalone proposition' and an 'according to' test. In the data README, Flagged means the task is malformed so that interpretability and attribution cannot be judged.

erman1980hearsay: the wording 'blackboard monitor', 'condition-action units' and 'limited processing resources to the most promising action first' was not confirmed; sources I found describe a 'focus-of-control mechanism' and control 'distributed heterarchically among the KSs'.

nii1986blackboard: the three-component wording and the jigsaw and koala examples were not confirmed by my searches (no full text). DBLP lists the article as 'Blackboard Systems, Part One', AI Magazine 7(2), pages 38-53.

stureborg2024inconsistent: the quoted sentence about a preference for self-generated text is presented in the poster as an implication of the perplexity bias ('An implication of this is ...'), not as a measured result. The poster is titled 'Limitations of Large Language Models as Automatic Evaluators'. The arXiv abstract could not be re-checked (search budget exhausted).

liu2023geval: the bias wording differs by version: arXiv v3 'potential issue', EMNLP version 'potential concern' of LLM-based evaluators having a bias towards LLM-generated texts. Spearman 0.514 confirmed at abstract level.

voorhees2000variations: search supports three judgment sets for TREC-4 and two for TREC-6, union and intersection qrels and Kendall's tau; the University of Waterloo detail is not confirmed. The URL listed in the summary's sources (ir.webis.de ... 98.39) is the SIGIR 1998 conference version, not the cited IP&M article.

choi2025debate: arXiv v1 lists the third author as 'Yixuan Li', v2 and the NeurIPS page 'Sharon Li' (as in the bib). Local models sampled at temperature 1.0 confirmed in src/model/model_utils.py. The 'round 0 is scored as majority vote' detail was not separately re-read by me; majority with random tie-break and the defaults (5 agents, 5 rounds) are confirmed.

gao2023alce: prompts/asqa_default.json holds 4 demonstrations (the pool); the paper prepends 2 sampled from that pool, consistent with the summary. The instruction also says 'Cite at least one document and at most three documents in each sentence' and eval.py evaluates only the first 3 citations by default.

du2024debate: the most-frequent-answer aggregation is in the GSM and MMLU evaluation scripts and the arithmetic script; the biography task has no majority step. Settings 3x2 and 2x3 and the 'largely for computational reasons' sentence are confirmed.
